abstract: Across species, individuals differ in their reliance on declarative versus procedural long-term memory systems for exploring and controlling the environment, mapping respectively onto allocentric place versus egocentric response learning strategies in a spatial navigation task. Several factors motivate the widely held consideration that procedural spatial learning strategies are generalisable to stimulus-response habits in the domain of instrumental conditioning, and vice versa; however, this hypothesis has received little empirical testing. Here, in a prospective longitudinal study of 72 rats (36 females), each animal was characterised for its place/response learning tendency using a dual-solution T-maze task and a 'direct opposition' test. Rats were then instrumentally conditioned to lever-press for food under a variable interval (VI) 60s schedule of reinforcement for five (Experiment 1) or 20 (Experiment 2) daily sessions, and the associative nature of their responding was assessed via sensitivity to offline reinforcer devaluation by pre-feeding to satiety. Against our hypothesis, response learners were less prone than place learners to rely on stimulus-response habits, an effect confined to female rats. Taken together, these findings reveal a complex, sex-dependent relationship between declarative and procedural memory systems and the two-fold associative basis of instrumental behaviour.
